content: The analysis of the data reveals the following findings: 1. There was substantial heterogeneity in the studies, with an I-squared value of 71%. However, no serious concerns were identified regarding indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. 2. Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring was conducted in a nested cardiac study involving 33 children receiving dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-P) in one study. No serious imprecision or publication bias was noted. All observed QTc interval prolongations (using Fridericia’s correction) were asymptomatic, and no child in the DHA-P group had QTc values exceeding 500 ms. 3. Monthly sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) was well-tolerated, with minor symptoms reported in both the SP and placebo groups. No participants discontinued the study medication. A slight increase in the QTc interval was observed after the third dose in 33 participants, but all cases were asymptomatic. 4. Based on data from 144,422 participants in one randomized controlled trial (RCT), mass drug administration (MDA) may reduce clinical malaria incidence in moderate-to-high transmission areas within 1–3 months post-MDA. However, the certainty of evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. 5. In low-to-very-low malaria transmission areas, MDA may reduce clinical malaria incidence within 1–3 months post-MDA, based on data from 130,651 participants in two studies. However, the evidence is of low certainty due to very serious imprecision. 6. The effect of MDA on clinical malaria incidence in low-to-very-low transmission areas 4–12 months post-MDA is uncertain, as the evidence is of very low certainty due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 7. MDA may slightly reduce Plasmodium falciparum parasite prevalence in moderate-to-high transmission areas 1–3 months post-MDA, based on data from 786 participants in one study. However, the evidence is of low certainty due to very serious imprecision. 8. MDA may have little or no effect on Plasmodium vivax parasite prevalence 4–12 months post-MDA, based on data from 6,255 participants in five studies. The evidence is of low certainty due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. 9. Serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported in several studies. For example, one study reported no SAEs, while another reported two SAEs (a serious skin reaction and severe anemia). Other studies reported SAEs such as dehydration, stillbirth, and miscarriage, but most were deemed unrelated to the drug. Mild adverse events, such as dizziness and rash, were more common. 10. Drug resistance was assessed in one study, where PfKelch13 mutations were identified in a small number of Plasmodium falciparum infections post-MDA. However, the evidence is limited and imprecise. 11. The effect of MDA on all-cause mortality in all ages and in children under five years remains uncertain due to very low certainty of evidence, serious risk of bias, and imprecision. 12. Hospital admissions for all causes decreased by 5–21% during the four weeks following the first round of MDA and by 8–19% after the second round. However, statistical significance was observed at only one of eight time points, and data from non-MDA control areas were unavailable. 13. MDA with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and artesunate, with or without primaquine, probably increases vomiting, based on moderate-certainty evidence. 14. MDA may improve hemoglobin levels between day 1 and day 7 post-treatment in low-to-very-low transmission settings, based on high-certainty evidence. 15. Overall, the certainty of evidence for many outcomes is limited by serious risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision, highlighting the need for further high-quality research to clarify the effects of MDA on malaria-related outcomes.
